title: Made All Day, Held Back Until Stress

scenes.visual: Dark slate background (#0F172A). A clean cell cross-section fills 70% of frame height (schematic): a steady stream of teal p53 blocks emerges from a synthesis spout on the left, while amber MDM2 clamps whisk them into a spinning amber proteasome ring. Title 'Made All Day, Held Back Until Stress' appears in crisp white (size 42) at top centre and fades gently out.

scenes.tts: Your cells build p fifty-three all day long and shred half of each new batch within about twenty minutes. Why make a guardian only to destroy it? Because an emergency cannot wait for a gene to be read and a protein built. When the responder already exists, the cell only has to let go.
scenes.caption: Your cells build p53 all day long and shred half of each new batch within about twenty minutes. Why make a guardian only to destroy it? Because an emergency cannot wait for a gene to be read and a protein built. When the responder already exists, the cell only has to let go.
scenes.visual: Same cell cross-section carried in place. Teal p53 blocks flow steadily from the synthesis spout (labelled 'p53 synthesis', size 28, teal) while amber clamps drag half of them into the proteasome ring as a small 20-minute timer sweeps halfway round. A slow dim grey gene-to-protein progress bar appears briefly at bottom to contrast waiting for transcription, then fades.
scenes.narration: Your cells build p53 all day long and shred half of each new batch within about twenty minutes. Why make a guardian only to destroy it? Because an emergency cannot wait for a gene to be read and a protein built. When the responder already exists, the cell only has to let go.

scenes.tts: p fifty-three is a transcription factor, a protein that binds DNA to turn genes on. In a calm cell, a partner called M D M two grips it and covers its active end. M D M two also tags it with ubiquitin, a mark sending proteins to the proteasome shredder.
scenes.caption: p53 is a transcription factor, a protein that binds DNA to turn genes on. In a calm cell, a partner called MDM2 grips it and covers its active end. MDM2 also tags it with ubiquitin, a mark sending proteins to the proteasome shredder.
scenes.visual: Zoom smoothly on the teal p53 block inside the same cell frame, showing a labelled 'gene-activation end' and 'DNA-binding end' (schematic). An amber MDM2 clamp slides over the gene-activation end, attaches a chain of small amber ubiquitin beads (labelled 'ubiquitin'), and carries p53 into the rotating proteasome ring, where p53 dissolves into small fading dots.
scenes.narration: p53 is a transcription factor, a protein that binds DNA to turn genes on. In a calm cell, a partner called MDM2 grips it and covers its active end. MDM2 also tags it with ubiquitin, a mark sending proteins to the proteasome shredder.

scenes.tts: Why does steady shredding give speed? At balance, when making equals destroying, protein level equals synthesis rate divided by the destruction rate constant. Suppose synthesis adds eighty units an hour, and the destruction constant is four per hour. Eighty divided by four leaves twenty units at rest. Cut the constant fourfold, to one, and eighty divided by one gives eighty units, with no new gene read.
scenes.caption: Why does steady shredding give speed? At balance, when making equals destroying, protein level equals synthesis rate divided by the destruction rate constant. Suppose synthesis adds 80 units an hour, and the destruction constant is 4 per hour. 80 ÷ 4 = 20 units at rest. Cut the constant fourfold, to 1, and 80 ÷ 1 = 80 units, with no new gene read.
scenes.visual: The cell cross-section shifts slightly left while a large vertical teal level gauge (0 to 100 units, computed curve labelled 'schematic units') slides into the right third. Above the gauge appears the formula 'level = synthesis ÷ destruction' (size 30, white). As spoken, '80 ÷ 4 = 20' builds piece by piece with the gauge hovering at 20; then the amber shredder ring slows 4×, '4' morphs into '1', and the computed exponential curve climbs smoothly from 20 toward 80 while the teal synthesis stream stays completely unchanged.
scenes.narration: Why does steady shredding give speed? At balance, when making equals destroying, protein level equals synthesis rate divided by the destruction rate constant. Suppose synthesis adds 80 units an hour, and the destruction constant is 4 per hour. 80 ÷ 4 = 20 units at rest. Cut the constant fourfold, to 1, and 80 ÷ 1 = 80 units, with no new gene read.

scenes.tts: Now radiation snaps both strands of DNA. That break activates a kinase called A T M, an enzyme that adds phosphate tags. A T M and downstream kinases tag both M D M two and p fifty-three. M D M two's grip loosens, destruction drops, and p fifty-three climbs fast, switching on genes that pause division and start repair.
scenes.caption: Now radiation snaps both strands of DNA. That break activates a kinase called ATM, an enzyme that adds phosphate tags. ATM and downstream kinases tag both MDM2 and p53. MDM2's grip loosens, destruction drops, and p53 climbs fast, switching on genes that pause division and start repair.
scenes.visual: Inside the nucleus at top-left of the same cell, a coral lightning flash snaps a DNA double-strand bar into two pieces. A coral ATM kinase block lights up at the break and launches glowing coral 'P' phosphate badges onto both amber MDM2 and teal p53. The amber clamp pops open and drifts away; the teal gauge on the right shoots up from 20 to 80 without any change in the synthesis spout, and teal p53 blocks move onto DNA bars labelled 'p21 (pause)' and 'DNA repair'.
scenes.narration: Now radiation snaps both strands of DNA. That break activates a kinase called ATM, an enzyme that adds phosphate tags. ATM and downstream kinases tag both MDM2 and p53. MDM2's grip loosens, destruction drops, and p53 climbs fast, switching on genes that pause division and start repair.

scenes.tts: Many stress pathways hold responders back until stress removes the restraint. Broken DNA has a dedicated kinase sensor. Now imagine dozens of unrelated toxic chemicals entering the cell instead. How could one protein detect an entire chemical class without a custom pocket for each toxin? Pause and predict.
scenes.caption: Many stress pathways hold responders back until stress removes the restraint. Broken DNA has a dedicated kinase sensor. Now imagine dozens of unrelated toxic chemicals entering the cell instead. How could one protein detect an entire chemical class without a custom pocket for each toxin? Pause and predict.
scenes.visual: The DNA break fades and the same cell cross-section now faces a cloud of varied coral shapes (triangles, wedges, rings, labelled 'diverse chemical threats', size 28) crossing the membrane. An amber catcher block sits in the cytosol with a bold white question card at top: 'How can one sensor detect dozens of differently shaped toxins?'
scenes.narration: Many stress pathways hold responders back until stress removes the restraint. Broken DNA has a dedicated kinase sensor. Now imagine dozens of unrelated toxic chemicals entering the cell instead. How could one protein detect an entire chemical class without a custom pocket for each toxin? Pause and predict.

scenes.visual: The question card remains clearly visible at top centre while the varied coral chemical shapes drift slowly around the amber catcher block and a soft 4.5-second progress bar fills smoothly along the bottom edge.

scenes.tts: The sensor works by being attacked. Many chemical threats are electrophiles, molecules hungry for electrons. Their responder, N R F two, is made all day and turns on protective enzymes. A partner called Keap one normally passes it to the shredder. Keap one carries cysteines whose sulfur atoms give up electrons easily, so electrophiles react with them. It reads electron hunger, not shape.
scenes.caption: The sensor works by being attacked. Many chemical threats are electrophiles, molecules hungry for electrons. Their responder, Nrf2, is made all day and turns on protective enzymes. A partner called Keap1 normally passes it to the shredder. Keap1 carries cysteines whose sulfur atoms give up electrons easily, so electrophiles react with them. It reads electron hunger, not shape.
scenes.visual: Question card fades. The synthesis spout now emits teal Nrf2 blocks (labelled 'Nrf2', size 28) gripped by amber Keap1 catchers (labelled 'Keap1', schematic) studded with glowing yellow-amber sulfur-tipped 'Cys' knobs (cysteines). Coral electrophile shapes collide with and bond covalently to those sulfur knobs, flashing brightly on impact to show chemical reaction rather than lock-and-key shape fit.
scenes.narration: The sensor works by being attacked. Many chemical threats are electrophiles, molecules hungry for electrons. Their responder, Nrf2, is made all day and turns on protective enzymes. A partner called Keap1 normally passes it to the shredder. Keap1 carries cysteines whose sulfur atoms give up electrons easily, so electrophiles react with them. It reads electron hunger, not shape.

scenes.tts: On the current view, altered Keap one stops passing N R F two for destruction. With the catchers tied up, newly made N R F two escapes straight to the nucleus. Other pathways reuse this trick, holding intact kinases or folding sensors quiet until stress arrives.
scenes.caption: On the current view, altered Keap1 stops passing Nrf2 for destruction. With the catchers tied up, newly made Nrf2 escapes straight to the nucleus. Other pathways reuse this trick, holding intact kinases or folding sensors quiet until stress arrives.
scenes.visual: Modified amber Keap1 catchers stay bound to older teal Nrf2 blocks without passing them to the proteasome, visibly filling the Keap1 pool. Fresh teal Nrf2 blocks streaming from the synthesis spout bypass the full catchers, enter the nucleus, and light up a teal 'protective enzymes' bar while the right-hand gauge climbs. Along the bottom, two small schematic badges appear and settle: 'ASK1 + thioredoxin' and 'ER sensors + BiP', each with an amber restraint lifting off a teal block.
scenes.narration: On the current view, altered Keap1 stops passing Nrf2 for destruction. With the catchers tied up, newly made Nrf2 escapes straight to the nucleus. Other pathways reuse this trick, holding intact kinases or folding sensors quiet until stress arrives.

scenes.tts: Put both systems side by side. Building responders ahead costs energy, but buys minutes when danger strikes. Lifting a ready restraint lets the cell answer stress right away.
scenes.caption: Put both systems side by side. Building responders ahead costs energy, but buys minutes when danger strikes. Lifting a ready restraint lets the cell answer stress right away.
scenes.visual: Clean side-by-side view inside the same slate frame: left panel shows teal p53 freed from amber MDM2 by coral ATM phosphates; right panel shows newly made teal Nrf2 bypassing coral-modified amber Keap1. Both teal gauges sit high while both amber restraints are lifted.
scenes.narration: Put both systems side by side. Building responders ahead costs energy, but buys minutes when danger strikes. Lifting a ready restraint lets the cell answer stress right away.

scenes.visual: Clean dark slate end card showing one line only in bright white (size 40), centred: 'Many stress pathways hold responders back until stress removes the restraint.'
